html:
Equilibrium is the chapter that joins the arithmetic of Unit 1 to the acid–base and solubility work of the rest of the paper.

It carries about two questions, and they come in four shapes: a Kc or Kp calculation from equilibrium concentrations, a "which way does it shift" question on Le Chatelier, a pH or pKa one-liner, and a buffer, hydrolysis or Ksp judgement.

Almost every question is decided by one of two sentences — the equilibrium constant changes only with temperature and compare the ionic product with Ksp — so learn those two properly and the rest is arithmetic.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Equilibrium is dynamic: at equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and the concentrations stay constant, but both reactions continue.
  • K_c and K_p from the balanced equation, products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; pure solids and pure liquids never appear in the expression.
  • K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}, with \Delta n = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants). \Delta n = 0 makes K_p = K_c, and both are then dimensionless.
  • Q vs K: Q < K shifts forward, Q > K shifts backward, Q = K is equilibrium.
  • Le Chatelier: concentration, pressure (only if \Delta n \neq 0) and temperature; a catalyst never shifts an equilibrium and never changes K.
  • Definitions: Arrhenius (H⁺/OH⁻), Brønsted–Lowry (proton donor/acceptor, conjugate pairs), Lewis (electron-pair acceptor/donor); Ostwald's dilution law \alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}.
  • K_w = 10^{-14} at 25 °C, \text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14, \text{p}K_a + \text{p}K_b = 14; the log arithmetic for pH without a calculator.
  • Buffer: \text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}; the four salt types and which gives pH < 7, = 7, > 7.
  • K_{sp}: precipitation starts when the ionic product exceeds K_{sp}; for AB, s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}, for AB₂, K_{sp} = 4s^3.

7.1 Physical and chemical equilibrium; law of mass action; Kc, Kp and Q

Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

A reversible reaction can go in both directions under the same conditions; it is written with a double arrow, ⇌. Nothing is ever "finished": as soon as products appear they begin to react back.

A irreversible reaction, written with a single arrow, runs to completion — Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) in a test tube, or the burning of methane.

Dynamic equilibrium

A system is at dynamic equilibrium when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so that the concentrations of all species remain constant with time, although both reactions are still taking place.

Three ideas in that sentence carry marks. Equal rates, not equal concentrations. Constant concentrations, not zero rates.

Closed system — if a product escapes, as CO₂ does from an open flask of limestone, the reverse reaction cannot keep up and the "equilibrium" is never reached.

Feature What it means
Rates r_{\text{forward}} = r_{\text{reverse}} (not zero)
Concentrations constant in time, but generally not equal to each other
Starting point the same equilibrium position is reached whether you start from reactants or from products
Catalyst equilibrium is reached faster, at the same position
Nature dynamic, not static — measurable by isotopic labelling (H₂ + D₂ ⇌ 2HD)

The law of chemical equilibrium follows: at a fixed temperature, for

aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD

the ratio \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b} is constant at equilibrium. That constant is K_c, the equilibrium constant in terms of concentration.

The law of mass action

Law of mass action (Guldberg and Waage, 1864)

The rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient.

Applied to the forward and reverse reactions separately and then equated at equilibrium, the law gives the equilibrium constant:

K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b} \qquad K_p = \frac{p_C^{\,c}\,p_D^{\,d}}{p_A^{\,a}\,p_B^{\,b}}

where square brackets mean mol L⁻¹ and p means partial pressure (usually in atm). K_p is used for gas reactions because partial pressures are what a pressure change actually alters.

Rule for writing any K Example
products on top, reactants below N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ gives K_c = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3}
each concentration raised to its coefficient the 3 on H₂ becomes a cube, not a factor of 3
omit pure solids and pure liquids CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) gives K_p = p_{\text{CO}_2} only
omit the solvent in a dilute solution water is left out of the esterification constant
the reverse reaction has 1/K if K = 49 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, then K = 1/49 for 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂
doubling the equation squares K 2H₂ + 2I₂ ⇌ 4HI has K = 49^2 = 2401
Why solids and liquids are left out

The "concentration" of a pure solid or a pure liquid is its density divided by its molar mass — a fixed number at a given temperature. It is constant, so it is folded into K.

That is why a heap of CaCO₃ and a heap of CaO of any size give the same K_p: only p_{\text{CO}_2} appears. Writing [\text{CaCO}_3] in the expression is one of the most common wrong options in the paper.

The relation between Kp and Kc

K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}

We start from the ideal-gas law and substitute p = (n/V)RT = cRT for every gas.

Setting up. For aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD, all species gaseous, let \Delta n = (c + d) - (a + b), counting gases only.

Step 1 — replace each partial pressure. p_C = [C]RT, and likewise for the others.

Step 2 — substitute into K_p.

K_p = \frac{([C]RT)^c([D]RT)^d}{([A]RT)^a([B]RT)^b}

Step 3 — collect the powers of RT.

K_p = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b} \times (RT)^{(c+d)-(a+b)}

Step 4 — recognise K_c.

K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}

Result. K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}, with R = 0.0821\ \text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} when pressures are in atm, and T in kelvin.

What it means. The two constants differ only by the pressure–concentration conversion for the change in the number of gas molecules. If the reaction produces as many gas molecules as it consumes, \Delta n = 0, (RT)^0 = 1, and K_p = K_c exactly.

Reaction \Delta n K_p in terms of K_c Units of K_c Units of K_p
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ 2 − 4 = −2 K_c(RT)^{-2} L² mol⁻² atm⁻²
PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ 2 − 1 = +1 K_c(RT) mol L⁻¹ atm
H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI 2 − 2 = 0 K_c none none
N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ +1 K_c(RT) mol L⁻¹ atm
CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) 1 − 0 = +1 K_c(RT) mol L⁻¹ atm
The units question

The unit of K_c is (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{\Delta n} and of K_p is (\text{atm})^{\Delta n}. So for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, \Delta n = -2 and the unit is (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{-2} = \text{L}^2\text{mol}^{-2}.

When \Delta n = 0 the constant is dimensionless — a favourite one-mark question. A "unitless" answer is wrong for PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ and right for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI.

Kc from equilibrium concentrations, then Kp

Problem. At 500 K, 1.0 mol of N₂ and 3.0 mol of H₂ are sealed in a 1.0 L vessel. At equilibrium the vessel contains 1.0 mol N₂, 2.0 mol H₂ and 4.0 mol NH₃. Find K_c and K_p (R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

Solution. All volumes are 1.0 L, so moles = concentrations. K_c = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3} = \dfrac{4.0^2}{1.0 \times 2.0^3} = \dfrac{16}{8} = 2.0, unit L² mol⁻². \Delta n = 2 - 4 = -2, so K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2} = 2.0 \times (0.0821 \times 500)^{-2} = 2.0 \times (41.05)^{-2} = 1.19 \times 10^{-3} atm⁻².

The reaction quotient Q and the direction of shift

Q is the same fraction as K but built from concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium. Comparing the two tells you which way the reaction must go.

Comparison Meaning What happens
Q < K too little product, too much reactant reaction goes forward (to the right)
Q > K too much product reaction goes backward (to the left)
Q = K the ratio already has the equilibrium value the system is at equilibrium
Deciding the direction from Q

Problem. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K_c = 49 at 700 K. A mixture contains [H₂] = 1.0, [I₂] = 1.0 and [HI] = 2.0 mol L⁻¹. Which way does the reaction go?

Solution. Q = \dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]} = \dfrac{2.0^2}{1.0 \times 1.0} = 4.0. Q < K (4 < 49), so the reaction proceeds forward, making more HI until Q rises to 49.

What does and does not change K

K is a constant at a given temperature and nothing else. This one sentence answers a large share of the objective questions on the chapter.

Change Effect on K Effect on the position
temperature changes (increases for endothermic, decreases for exothermic) shifts
adding or removing a reactant or product none shifts to restore Q = K
changing pressure or volume none shifts only if \Delta n \neq 0
adding a catalyst none none — equilibrium arrives sooner
adding an inert gas at constant volume none none
changing the surface area of a solid none none
Reading a "K changes?" question

Underline the word constant. If the only change is concentration, pressure, volume, catalyst or surface area, K does not move — only the position does. Temperature is the sole entry in the left-hand column that changes K.

7.2 Le Chatelier's principle and its applications

Le Chatelier's principle (1884)

If a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the system shifts in the direction that tends to oppose the change and so establishes a new equilibrium.

Disturbance Shift Reason
add a reactant forward uses up the added substance
remove a product forward replaces what was taken away
add a product backward removes the added product
increase pressure (reduce volume) towards the side with fewer gas molecules fewer molecules occupy less space
decrease pressure towards more gas molecules
increase temperature in the endothermic direction absorbs the extra heat
decrease temperature in the exothermic direction releases heat
add catalyst no shift forward and reverse rates rise equally

Two cases where students lose the mark:

  • \Delta n = 0. In H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI there are two gas molecules on each side, so squeezing the mixture changes both partial pressures equally and the position does not move at all. Pressure has no effect.
  • Inert gas. Added at constant volume, it does not change any partial pressure and there is no shift. Added at constant pressure the vessel must expand, every partial pressure falls, and the equilibrium shifts towards the side with more gas molecules — exactly as if the pressure had been lowered.

The Haber process

\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}

Factor Effect on yield of NH₃ What the industry does
pressure 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas, so high pressure favours NH₃ about 200 atm
temperature exothermic, so low temperature favours NH₃ about 700 K (430 °C)
catalyst no effect on yield, large effect on rate iron with K₂O and Al₂O₃ promoters
removal of NH₃ shifts forward cool and condense the ammonia, recycle the rest

Why a compromise temperature? At 300 K the equilibrium yield at 200 atm is very high but the reaction is so slow that the plant would produce almost nothing.

At 900 K the rate is excellent but the equilibrium has moved back towards nitrogen and hydrogen.

The catalyst only works efficiently above about 650 K. The operating temperature of about 700 K is therefore the point where a usable rate and a worthwhile yield meet — a compromise, not an optimum of either quantity alone.

Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium the right way and also raises the collision rate, which is why pressure is pushed as high as the plant's steel allows.

The contact process

2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -197\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}

Three gas molecules become two, and the reaction is exothermic, so high pressure and low temperature both favour SO₃.

Again the rate sets the limit: the plant runs at about 720 K (450 °C) and 1–2 atm over a V₂O₅ catalyst, with the SO₃ absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ as it forms so that it cannot react back. The yield is about 98 %.

The Ostwald process

4\text{NH}_3(g) + 5\text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 4\text{NO}(g) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad \Delta H = -905\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}

Here 9 gas molecules become 10, so a rise in pressure shifts the equilibrium backwards — pressure is not a lever for yield in this step.

It is still run at about 9 atm because the higher pressure raises the collision rate and the throughput, and because the equilibrium lies so far to the right at 800–900 K that the yield is nearly complete.

The real difficulty is selectivity: too high a temperature decomposes NH₃ and carries the oxidation on to N₂. Hence a platinum–rhodium gauze at about 800 K, a contact time of about a millisecond, and rapid cooling of the gases.

Catalyst, yield and K

A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions by the same amount. It therefore does not change \Delta H, does not change K, and does not change the equilibrium yield — it only shortens the time needed to reach it.

Every option that says "the catalyst increases the yield of ammonia" is wrong for that reason.

Using Le Chatelier on a real equilibrium

Problem. For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH = −197 kJ, state the effect on the amount of SO₃ of(a) raising the temperature,(b) compressing the mixture,(c) adding V₂O₅,(d) removing SO₃.

Solution.(a) The forward reaction is exothermic, so heat is a product; raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium backward and SO₃ falls.(b) 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas, so compression shifts forward and SO₃ rises.(c) No effect on the amount — equilibrium is reached sooner only.(d) Removing a product shifts the equilibrium forward, so more SO₃ forms (and the yield of the step rises).

7.3 Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis acids and bases; Ostwald's dilution law

The three definitions

Theory Acid Base Example that only this theory explains
Arrhenius (1884) gives H⁺ ions in water gives OH⁻ ions in water HCl and NaOH in water
Brønsted–Lowry (1923) proton (H⁺) donor proton acceptor NH₃ is a base although it contains no OH
Lewis (1923) electron-pair acceptor electron-pair donor BF₃ + NH₃, with no proton transferred at all

Each theory widens the one before. Arrhenius cannot call NH₃ a base (it has no OH group) and cannot handle reactions in solvents other than water.

Brønsted–Lowry handles NH₃ and all proton transfers, but cannot explain why BF₃ and AlCl₃ behave as acids. Lewis covers those, at the cost of calling every cation and every electron-pair-deficient molecule an acid.

Brønsted–Lowry acid and base

An acid is a species that donates a proton; a base is a species that accepts a proton. Every acid has a conjugate base, formed by losing one H⁺, and every base has a conjugate acid, formed by gaining one H⁺.

Acid Conjugate base Base Conjugate acid
HCl Cl⁻ NH₃ NH₄⁺
CH₃COOH CH₃COO⁻ OH⁻ H₂O
H₂O OH⁻ H₂O H₃O⁺
HCO₃⁻ CO₃²⁻ HCO₃⁻ H₂CO₃
NH₄⁺ NH₃ CH₃COO⁻ CH₃COOH
HSO₄⁻ SO₄²⁻ HSO₄⁻ H₂SO₄

A species that can both donate and accept a proton is amphiprotic — water, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻ and the amino acids are the standard examples.

Notice in the table that water appears twice: it is the base when it accepts a proton from HCl, and the acid when it donates one to NH₃.

The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. HCl is a strong acid, so Cl⁻ is a negligible base (which is why NaCl solutions are neutral); CH₃COOH is weak, so CH₃COO⁻ is a real base (which is why sodium acetate solutions are alkaline).

Strong and weak electrolytes

Degree of dissociation

The degree of dissociation \alpha is the fraction of the dissolved molecules that have split into ions: \alpha = \dfrac{\text{moles dissociated}}{\text{moles dissolved}}.

A strong electrolyte is almost completely dissociated (\alpha \approx 1); a weak electrolyte is only slightly dissociated (\alpha \ll 1).

Strong electrolyte Weak electrolyte
\alpha close to 1 (0.9–1) small (0.01–0.1)
Arrow single → double ⇌
Examples (acids) HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄ CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃, HCN, H₃PO₄, HF
Examples (bases) NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂ NH₃, amines, Mg(OH)₂
Examples (salts) NaCl, KNO₃, NH₄Cl (all soluble salts) — (salts are strong electrolytes)
Conductivity high low, but rises on dilution

Ostwald's dilution law

Ostwald's dilution law

We start from the equilibrium of a weak monobasic acid and the definition of \alpha.

Setting up. Let C mol L⁻¹ of HA be dissolved; a fraction \alpha dissociates.

\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-

Step 1 — concentrations at equilibrium. HA left = C(1-\alpha); [\text{H}^+] = [\text{A}^-] = C\alpha.

Step 2 — write K_a.

K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} = \frac{(C\alpha)(C\alpha)}{C(1-\alpha)} = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}

Step 3 — use the weakness. For a weak electrolyte \alpha \ll 1, so 1-\alpha \approx 1:

K_a = C\alpha^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{C}}

Result. \alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C} for a weak acid, and \alpha = \sqrt{K_b/C} for a weak base. The law holds only for weak binary electrolytes in dilute solution; it fails for strong electrolytes, where \alpha is near 1 and 1-\alpha cannot be dropped.

What it means. \alpha is inversely proportional to the square root of the concentration: diluting a weak acid increases the fraction dissociated.

Dilution raises α but lowers [H⁺]

These two statements look contradictory and examiners exploit the confusion.

As C falls, \alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C} rises, but the actual hydrogen-ion concentration [\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = \sqrt{K_aC} falls, because C falls faster than \alpha rises.

So a dilute weak acid is more dissociated and less acidic at the same time.

For acetic acid, K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}: at 0.1 M, \alpha = 1.3\% and [\text{H}^+] = 1.3 \times 10^{-3} M; at 0.001 M, \alpha = 13.4\% but [\text{H}^+] = 1.3 \times 10^{-4} M — ten times weaker.

Degree of dissociation and Ka

Problem. A 0.10 M solution of a weak monobasic acid has pH 2.87. Find \alpha and K_a.

Solution. [\text{H}^+] = 10^{-2.87} = 1.35 \times 10^{-3} M. \alpha = [\text{H}^+]/C = 1.35 \times 10^{-3}/0.10 = 1.35 \times 10^{-2} (1.35 %). K_a = C\alpha^2 = 0.10 \times (1.35 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}.

(Check with the shortcut: \alpha = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}/0.1} = 1.34\%.)

7.4 Ionic product of water, pH, pOH, pKa, pKb; common-ion effect; solubility product

The ionic product of water

Water dissociates very slightly:

\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-

K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} \ \text{at 25 °C}

K_w is the ionic product of water. Because dissociation absorbs heat, K_w increases with temperature — about 5.5 \times 10^{-13} at 100 °C.

Pure water is always electrically neutral, so [\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-7} M at 25 °C and pH 7. At 100 °C neutral water has pH ≈ 6.13: pH 7 means neutral only at 25 °C.

pH, pOH, pKa and pKb

\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+] \qquad \text{pOH} = -\log[\text{OH}^-] \qquad \text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14\ (25\ ^\circ\text{C})

\text{p}K_a = -\log K_a \qquad \text{p}K_b = -\log K_b \qquad \text{p}K_a + \text{p}K_b = 14\ \text{for a conjugate pair}

Solution [\text{H}^+] pH Working
0.01 M HCl 10^{-2} 2.00 strong acid, fully ionised
0.01 M NaOH 10^{-12} 12.00 pOH = 2, so pH = 14 − 2
2 \times 10^{-3} M HCl 2 \times 10^{-3} 2.70 3 − log 2 = 3 − 0.30
5 \times 10^{-5} M HCl 5 \times 10^{-5} 4.30 5 − log 5 = 5 − 0.70
0.1 M CH₃COOH 1.34 \times 10^{-3} 2.87 \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a - \log C)
0.1 M NH₃ 1.34 \times 10^{-3} (OH⁻) 11.13 pOH = 2.87, pH = 14 − 2.87
Log arithmetic without a calculator

Learn four logarithms and you can do every pH question in the paper by hand: \log 2 = 0.30, \log 3 = 0.48, \log 5 = 0.70, \log 7 = 0.85.

To take a pH, write the concentration as (a number between 1 and 10) × 10⁻ⁿ: the pH is n - \log(\text{that number}). So [\text{H}^+] = 4 \times 10^{-4} gives pH = 4 − 0.60 = 3.40.

Going the other way, pH 5.3 means [\text{H}^+] = 10^{-5.3} = 10^{-6} \times 10^{0.7} = 5 \times 10^{-6} M. For a weak acid use \text{pH} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a - \log C); for its salt, \text{pH} = 7 + \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a + \log C).

The common-ion effect

Common-ion effect

The common-ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte by the addition of a strong electrolyte that supplies one of the same ions.

Add sodium acetate to acetic acid. The acetate ion is already the product of the acid's ionisation, so by Le Chatelier the equilibrium is driven back to the left:

\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+

The result: \alpha falls, [\text{H}^+] falls, and the pH rises. The same idea lowers the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt in a solution containing one of its ions, and it is the reason a buffer works.

Common ion, by the Ka expression

Problem. Find the pH of a solution that is 0.10 M in CH₃COOH and 0.10 M in CH₃COONa (K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}).

Solution. The salt is fully ionised, so [\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] \approx 0.10 M. Let x = [\text{H}^+]. Then K_a = \dfrac{x(0.10 + x)}{0.10 - x} \approx \dfrac{x \times 0.10}{0.10}, so x = K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5} M and pH = 4.74.

Compare pure 0.10 M acetic acid: pH 2.87. The common ion has raised the pH by nearly two units — the acid is now only 0.018 % ionised.

Solubility product and precipitation

For a sparingly soluble salt in contact with its saturated solution,

\text{AgCl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \qquad K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Cl}^-]

Solubility product

The solubility product K_{sp} is the product of the molar concentrations of the ions in a saturated solution, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the dissociation equation, at a given temperature.

It is an equilibrium constant, so it depends only on temperature.

Salt Dissociation K_{sp} expression K_{sp} at 25 °C
AgCl AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Cl}^-] 1.8 \times 10^{-10}
AgBr AgBr(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Br⁻ [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Br}^-] 5.0 \times 10^{-13}
AgI AgI(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + I⁻ [\text{Ag}^+][\text{I}^-] 8.3 \times 10^{-17}
BaSO₄ BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ [\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}] 1.1 \times 10^{-10}
PbCl₂ PbCl₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ [\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^2 1.6 \times 10^{-5}
CaF₂ CaF₂(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻ [\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{F}^-]^2 4.0 \times 10^{-11}

The ionic product test. Calculate the ionic product Q_{sp} exactly as you would K_{sp}, but from the concentrations actually present:

Meaning Result
Q_{sp} < K_{sp} unsaturated no precipitate; more solid would dissolve
Q_{sp} = K_{sp} saturated at the point of precipitation
Q_{sp} > K_{sp} supersaturated precipitate forms until Q_{sp} falls to K_{sp}

Solubility from K_{sp}. Let the solubility be s mol L⁻¹.

Type Example K_{sp} Solubility
AB AgCl s^2 s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}
AB₂ or A₂B PbCl₂, Ag₂CrO₄ 4s^3 s = \sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}
AB₃ Fe(OH)₃ 27s^4 s = \sqrt[4]{K_{sp}/27}
Solubility of AgCl, and the common-ion effect on it

Problem. K_{sp}(\text{AgCl}) = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}. Find its solubility in(a) pure water and(b) 0.010 M NaCl. (M_{\text{AgCl}} = 143.5)

Solution.(a) s = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.34 \times 10^{-5} mol L⁻¹, which is 1.34 \times 10^{-5} \times 143.5 = 1.9 \times 10^{-3} g L⁻¹.(b) Now [\text{Cl}^-] = 0.010 M, so [\text{Ag}^+] = K_{sp}/0.010 = 1.8 \times 10^{-8} M. The solubility has fallen by a factor of about 750. This is the common-ion effect applied to a solubility equilibrium, and it is why AgCl is washed with dilute HCl, not water.

Will a precipitate form?

Problem. Equal volumes of 0.020 M AgNO₃ and 0.020 M NaCl are mixed. Will AgCl precipitate? (K_{sp} = 1.8 \times 10^{-10})

Solution. Mixing doubles the total volume, so each concentration is halved: [\text{Ag}^+] = [\text{Cl}^-] = 0.010 M. Q_{sp} = 0.010 \times 0.010 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}. Q_{sp} \gg K_{sp} (10^{-4} against 10^{-10}), so yes, AgCl precipitates at once.

Three Ksp traps
  1. K_{sp} has no units in the expression but the concentrations are molar. Do not add the concentrations; multiply them, with each raised to its coefficient.
  2. K_{sp} is not solubility. For salts of different types, the bigger K_{sp} does not always mean the more soluble salt — compare s, not K_{sp}.
  3. A precipitate needs Q_{sp} > K_{sp}, not Q_{sp} = K_{sp} and certainly not "K_{sp} is exceeded by the mass added". Calculate the concentrations after mixing, which means after any dilution.

7.5 Acidic and basic buffers; types of salts and their hydrolysis

Buffer solutions

Buffer

A buffer solution is a solution that resists a change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added, or when it is diluted. An acidic buffer contains a weak acid and its salt with a strong base; a basic buffer contains a weak base and its salt with a strong acid.

Acidic buffer Basic buffer
Contains weak acid + its salt (CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa) weak base + its salt (NH₃ + NH₄Cl)
pH below 7 (about \text{p}K_a) above 7 (about 14 - \text{p}K_b)
Added H⁺ is consumed by CH₃COO⁻ NH₃
Added OH⁻ is consumed by CH₃COOH NH₄⁺
Henderson form \text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} \text{pOH} = \text{p}K_b + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}

How it works. In an acetic acid–acetate buffer both components are present in large amount. Added H⁺ is taken up by the acetate ion, added OH⁻ is taken up by the acid, and neither survives to change the pH much.

The ratio [salt]/[acid] barely moves, so the pH barely moves.

Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

Setting up. A weak acid HA at concentration c_a with its salt NaA at c_s. The salt is fully ionised, so [\text{A}^-] \approx c_s; the acid is only slightly ionised, so [\text{HA}] \approx c_a.

Step 1 — start from K_a.

K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}

Step 2 — solve for [\text{H}^+].

[\text{H}^+] = K_a\frac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]} = K_a\frac{c_a}{c_s}

Step 3 — take negative logarithms of both sides.

-\log[\text{H}^+] = -\log K_a - \log\frac{c_a}{c_s}

Step 4 — use the definitions and flip the ratio.

\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\frac{c_s}{c_a}

Result. \text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}.

What it means. The pH is fixed by the ratio, not by the absolute concentrations, which is why dilution does not change the pH of a buffer much. When [\text{salt}] = [\text{acid}], pH = pKa — the point of maximum buffer capacity.

pH of an acetic acid–acetate buffer

Problem. A buffer is 0.10 M in CH₃COOH and 0.20 M in CH₃COONa; pKa = 4.74. Find its pH, and the pH after 0.01 mol of HCl is added to 1.0 L of it.

Solution. pH = 4.74 + \log(0.20/0.10) = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04. After adding 0.01 mol HCl, the acid rises to 0.11 M and the salt falls to 0.19 M: pH = 4.74 + \log(0.19/0.11) = 4.74 + 0.24 = 4.98.

The pH has moved by only 0.06 unit; the same amount of HCl in 1.0 L of pure water would take pH from 7 to 2.

Blood is buffered at pH 7.35–7.45 by the H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ pair (and by haemoglobin and phosphate); a deviation of 0.4 unit is life-threatening. Buffer capacity is greatest when the ratio is 1 : 1 and falls as the ratio moves away from it.

Salt hydrolysis — the four types

A salt of a weak acid or weak base reacts with water; this is hydrolysis. Which ion hydrolyses decides whether the solution is acidic, basic or neutral.

Salt type Example Ion that hydrolyses Solution pH formula
strong acid + strong base NaCl, KNO₃, Na₂SO₄ neither neutral, pH 7 pH = 7
weak acid + strong base CH₃COONa, Na₂CO₃, KCN the anion (A⁻) basic, pH > 7 \text{pH} = 7 + \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a + \log C)
strong acid + weak base NH₄Cl, (NH₄)₂SO₄ the cation (BH⁺) acidic, pH < 7 \text{pH} = 7 - \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_b + \log C)
weak acid + weak base CH₃COONH₄, NH₄CN both ions depends on K_a vs K_b \text{pH} = 7 + \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a - \text{p}K_b)

Why each behaves as it does.

  • NaCl. Na⁺ is the conjugate acid of NaOH (a strong base) and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of HCl (a strong acid). Neither is strong enough to take or give a proton to water, so nothing hydrolyses and the pH stays 7.
  • CH₃COONa. The acetate ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it does take a proton from water:

\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{OH}^-

OH⁻ is left over, so the solution is basic. The hydrolysis constant is K_h = K_w/K_a. - NH₄Cl. The ammonium ion is the conjugate acid of a weak base and donates a proton to water:

\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+

H₃O⁺ is produced, so the solution is acidic, with K_h = K_w/K_b. - CH₃COONH₄. Both ions hydrolyse.

Because K_a(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) \approx K_b(\text{NH}_3) \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-5}, the two effects cancel and the pH is 7.00 — and, unusually, independent of concentration.

pH of a salt of a weak acid

Problem. Find the pH of 0.10 M CH₃COONa (K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}, so pKa = 4.74).

Solution. pH = 7 + \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a + \log C) = 7 + \tfrac{1}{2}(4.74 - 1.00) = 7 + 1.87 = 8.87.

Check the logic the salt of a weak acid is basic, and 8.87 is basic but not strongly so.

pH of a salt of a weak base

Problem. Find the pH of 0.10 M NH₄Cl (K_b for NH₃ = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}).

Solution. pH = 7 - \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_b + \log C) = 7 - \tfrac{1}{2}(4.74 - 1.00) = 7 - 1.87 = 5.13. Acidic, as expected for the salt of a weak base.

The hydrolysis traps
  • pH 7 does not mean "no hydrolysis". It means the two hydrolyses happen to cancel (CH₃COONH₄) or that neither ion hydrolyses (NaCl). Read the question.
  • A salt of a weak acid is basic, not acidic. Students reverse this because the word "acid" appears. Anchor it: the anion of a weak acid is a base (it takes H⁺ back).
  • The pH of a weak acid–weak base salt does not depend on concentration, because the C cancels between the two hydrolysis expressions. Every formula with \log C in it must contain a \log C term that is genuinely there.
  • Hydrolysis increases on dilution and on heating (both are endothermic in the forward direction for these salts), so a dilute or warm salt solution is further from pH 7.

Chapter summary

  • At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant, but both reactions continue; a catalyst only shortens the time taken to get there.
  • K_c and K_p take products over reactants with each concentration raised to its coefficient; pure solids and pure liquids are omitted because their concentrations are constant.
  • K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}. When \Delta n = 0 the two are equal and both are dimensionless; when \Delta n = -2, K_c carries L² mol⁻² and K_p atm⁻².
  • Q is the same ratio at any moment: Q < K shifts forward, Q > K shifts backward. Only temperature changes K; pressure shifts the position only if \Delta n \neq 0.
  • Le Chatelier: added reactant, removed product, higher pressure (towards fewer gas moles) and lower temperature (for an exothermic reaction) all push the equilibrium forward. Haber, contact and Ostwald each use a compromise temperature of roughly 700–800 K for rate, with pressure chosen from \Delta n.
  • Arrhenius: H⁺/OH⁻ in water. Brønsted–Lowry: proton donor/acceptor, with conjugate pairs differing by one H⁺. Lewis: electron-pair acceptor/donor. Amphiprotic species (H₂O, HCO₃⁻) can act either way.
  • Ostwald's dilution law gives \alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}: dilution raises the fraction dissociated but lowers [\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}.
  • K_w = 10^{-14} at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, pKa + pKb = 14. Neutral is pH 7 only at 25 °C.
  • A buffer is a weak acid (or base) with its salt; \text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log([\text{salt}]/[\text{acid}]), and the pH depends on the ratio, not the concentrations.
  • Salt hydrolysis: strong/strong neutral; weak acid/strong base basic; strong acid/weak base acidic; weak/weak decided by K_a against K_b and independent of concentration.
  • K_{sp} is an equilibrium constant: a precipitate forms when the ionic product after mixing exceeds it, and a common ion lowers the solubility.

Model answer D1: chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle (10 marks)

Introduction. A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. The concentrations then remain constant, but the reaction is dynamic, not stopped.

Law of mass action. For aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD, K_c = \dfrac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}. K_p is the same expression in partial pressures. The relation is K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}, where \Delta n = (c + d) - (a + b) for gases. K_p = K_c when \Delta n = 0.

Reaction quotient. Q has the same form as K but uses the present concentrations. If Q < K, the reaction goes forward; if Q > K it goes backward; if Q = K it is at equilibrium.

Reversing the reaction gives 1/K, doubling the equation squares K, and adding two reactions multiplies their K values.

Le Chatelier's principle. If a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts to oppose the change.

Change Effect (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, \Delta H < 0)
Add N₂ or H₂ shifts forward
Remove NH₃ shifts forward
Increase pressure shifts to fewer moles (forward)
Raise temperature shifts to the endothermic (backward) side, and K falls
Add a catalyst no shift, equilibrium reached faster
Add an inert gas at constant V no change

Industrial use. In Haber's process, about 200 atm, 450 to 500^{\circ}\text{C} and an iron catalyst with a promoter give a good compromise between yield and rate.

Numerical. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI with K_c = 50, start with 1\ \text{mol} each in 1\ \text{L}. At equilibrium [\text{HI}] = 2x and [\text{H}_2] = [\text{I}_2] = 1 - x.

Then \dfrac{(2x)^2}{(1 - x)^2} = 50 gives \dfrac{2x}{1 - x} = 7.07, so x = 0.78, [\text{HI}] = 1.56\ \text{M} and [\text{H}_2] = [\text{I}_2] = 0.22\ \text{M}.

For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 500\ \text{K}, \Delta n = -2, so K_p = K_c(0.0821\times500)^{-2} = K_c/1685.

Conclusion. K depends only on temperature, and Le Chatelier's principle predicts the direction of the shift for a change in concentration, pressure or temperature.

Model answer D2: pH, buffers and solubility product (10 marks)

Introduction. Ionic equilibria involve weak acids and bases (partial ionisation) and sparingly soluble salts.

pH. \text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+], \text{pOH} = -\log[\text{OH}^-], and \text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14 at 25^{\circ}\text{C} (K_w = 10^{-14}).

For a weak acid K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} and [\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_aC} (when \alpha \ll 1), with the degree of ionisation \alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C} (Ostwald's dilution law).

Also K_aK_b = K_w for a conjugate pair.

Acid-base theories. Arrhenius (H⁺/OH⁻), Brønsted-Lowry (proton donor/acceptor, conjugate pairs) and Lewis (electron pair acceptor/donor).

Buffer solutions resist a change in pH on adding small amounts of acid or base. They are a weak acid with its salt (acetic acid and sodium acetate, acidic buffer) or a weak base with its salt (NH₄OH and NH₄Cl).

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is \text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}. The buffer capacity is greatest when [\text{salt}] = [\text{acid}]. Blood (H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻, pH 7.4) is a natural buffer.

Solubility product. For A_xB_y \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}, K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x[B^{x-}]^y. A precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds K_{sp}.

For a salt of type AB, s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}, for type AB₂, s = \sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}. The common ion effect lowers the solubility of a salt by adding an ion it already has, which is the basis of qualitative analysis.

Salt type Example K_{sp} in terms of s
AB AgCl s^2
AB₂ Ca(OH)₂, PbCl₂ 4s^3
AB₃ Al(OH)₃ 27s^4

Numerical.

  • 0.1\ \text{M} acetic acid (K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}): [\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-6}} = 1.34\times10^{-3}\ \text{M}, pH = 2.87, and \alpha = 1.3\%.
  • A buffer of 0.1\ \text{M} acid and 0.1\ \text{M} acetate has \text{pH} = \text{p}K_a = 4.74. With 0.2\ \text{M} acetate it is 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04.
  • AgCl (K_{sp} = 1.8\times10^{-10}): s = 1.34\times10^{-5}\ \text{M} in water but only 1.8\times10^{-9}\ \text{M} in 0.1\ \text{M} NaCl.

Conclusion. K_a gives pH of weak acids, the Henderson equation gives buffer pH, and K_{sp} predicts precipitation and the common ion effect.
